How to Care for Your Aquarium Fish During a Power Outage - Aquarium Co-Op
Máy sủi oxy có tốn điện không? Có nên bật liên tục cho hồ cá?

facts.fact: An air pump sits outside the tank and pushes air through airline tubing. Only the last piece of tubing goes into the water, where it connects to an air stone, a sponge filter or another air-driven device.
Aeration works by moving the water surface: carbon dioxide leaves the water and oxygen from the air dissolves in.
Aquarium Co-Op's tests found that more gas exchange at the water surface raised oxygen levels, while a circulation pump alone did not noticeably raise them.
Aquarium Co-Op says oxygen in a freshwater tank should ideally be around 7 to 8 ppm (mg/L).
Aquarium Co-Op recommends at least one air source in every aquarium, whatever other filtration it has.
Rising bubbles stir up turbulent flow, and that turbulence is what gives strong aeration.
A smooth water surface gives only about 5% of the aeration of a choppy surface of the same size.
Fully oxygen-saturated water at 78°F holds about 8.25 ppm. Warmer water holds less oxygen than cold water.
Water at 78°F is not necessarily saturated with oxygen, so extra aeration still helps at any temperature.
An air pump can also drive a sponge filter, where air lifts water through a sponge to give mechanical and biological filtration.
Signs of low oxygen include fish resting near the bottom, eating less, breathing fast with their gills, or gasping at the surface.
In tanks with little current, oxygen-starved fish hang near the surface, breathe fast and 'pipe' at the surface. In tanks with strong current, they swim with their mouths gaping.
Common causes of low oxygen include high temperatures, overstocking, some medications or chemical treatments, and too little movement at the surface.
If a tank is short of oxygen, Aquarium Co-Op advises starting with a large water change, then finding and fixing the cause.
If an air pump falls into water, unplug it at once and do not reach in for it.
Fit a check valve on the airline so water cannot flow back into the tubing.
Hikari says to install the FujiMAC pump higher than the water level so water cannot flow back into it.
Hikari says to put the FujiMAC pump on a level surface, out of direct sunlight, in a well-ventilated spot that is easy to reach.

Fluval's manual says to take the airline off the pump's outlet before unplugging the pump, so water cannot siphon back into it. If the tubing cannot be removed first, raise the pump above the water level.
Airflow on the EHEIM air pumps can be adjusted at each outlet and at the air stone (diffuser).
Air stones give very fine bubbles and are quieter than bubblers that release bigger bubbles.

Maintenance: Fluval's manual says its A-series pump needs no regular internal maintenance, but the rest of the air system (air stones, tubing, ornaments) should be checked and cleaned from time to time.
Maintenance: Fluval says to wipe the outside of the pump with a soft, damp cloth, and never to put the pump in water or use detergents.
Maintenance: Clogged air stones or other blockages build back pressure that can stretch or tear the diaphragm. A stretched diaphragm gives less air, and a torn one stops the air entirely.
Troubleshooting: If no air comes out, Fluval says to check the power, then check the hose and valves for blockages, then disconnect the line to see whether the pump itself is giving air.
Troubleshooting: Fluval says a torn or weakened diaphragm is the most common reason a pump gives no air.
Maintenance: Hikari says to replace the FujiMAC diaphragm/valve every year, and to clean the air filter every 3 or 4 months and replace it yearly.
Maintenance: Hikari says to unplug the FujiMAC pump and let it cool before opening the cover or doing any maintenance, because it gets extremely hot while running.
Power use: EHEIM rates its air100 (100 l/h) and air200 (200 l/h) aquarium air pumps at 3.5 W, and its air400 (400 l/h) at 4 W, at 50 Hz.
Power use: Hikari's FujiMAC pond air pumps draw from 24 watts (40K model) up to 250 watts (300K model).
Sizing: Air stones work well only if the pump is big enough to make hundreds of bubbles per second. The small pumps that come with kits are described as too weak.
In dry climates, air pumps with air stones can carry moisture out of the tank and increase evaporation. The page suggests choppy-surface aeration there instead.
The air going into the tank must be clean: aerosols, chemicals and fumigation gases drawn in can kill fish.
Do not let floating plants cover the whole surface, because that reduces gas exchange.
Long, shallow tanks have more surface area than tall, narrow ones, which helps gas exchange.
Power cut: In the first 1–2 hours, Aquarium Co-Op advises not feeding, not changing water and not making sudden changes, and using the time to find backup power.
Power cut: After 8 or more hours without power, run the air pump for 1 hour every 8 hours. Heavily stocked tanks, or fish gasping at the surface, may need aeration every 4 hours.
Power cut: A USB air pump can run on a USB power bank or a laptop. A larger linear piston pump can run on a large power bank or a car battery inverter.

Power cut: Aquarium Co-Op says its air pump with battery backup switches on by itself when the power fails and runs about 20 hours nonstop, or 40 hours or more in Power Save mode (15 seconds on, 15 seconds off). Lowering the airflow makes it last longer.
Power cut in hot weather: Move the tank to a cooler, shaded spot and use a battery fan blowing across the surface. Do not float ice, because fast temperature changes stress fish.
After a power cut: Do not feed for the first 24 hours after the power returns, and test for ammonia and nitrite, doing water changes if either is above 0 ppm.
Plugging hang-on-back or canister filters back in after a long power cut without cleaning them can flush rotting debris into the tank. Clean them first.
Air pump brands named by a Vietnamese aquarium shop include Resun, Atman, Sunsun and Hailea. In Vietnamese an air pump is called 'máy sủi oxy'.
Aquariumscience.org calls the '12 square inches of surface per inch of fish' rule a myth: a 2-inch fish needs eight times the aeration of a 1-inch fish.
Aquariumscience.org rejects the claim that diffusion alone, without surface movement, gives enough oxygen for a tank with a fair number of fish.
